tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The analyst who prepared the briefing joined the call late.
The report which the committee rejected it contained outdated figures.
The bakery who opened last month already has a waiting list.
The contract that legal signed yesterday takes effect on Monday.
The stadium, that was renovated in 2019, hosted the finals.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Who" correctly refers to a person in a restrictive clause that defines which analyst you mean.

Tip: For people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" both work; pick one and stay consistent.

FALSE — Drop the extra "it": the relative already stands for the object, so write "which the committee rejected."

Tip: Never leave a leftover pronoun after a relative clause that already fills that slot.

FALSE — A bakery is a thing, so use "which" (or "that"), not "who."

Tip: Reserve "who" for people (and sometimes organisations treated as people in formal writing).

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which contract; no commas needed.

Tip: No commas = the clause is essential to identify the noun.

FALSE — After commas (non-restrictive), use "which," not "that": "The stadium, which was renovated…"

Tip: Commas signal extra information — and "that" is not welcome there.
tasks.solution_overview: Start by asking whether the clause names a person or a thing, and whether the commas mark it as essential or extra. Then check that the relative itself carries the subject or object — no leftover "it" or "them." A quick who/which/that pass catches most early mistakes.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The manager whose team hit the target received a bonus.
The auditor who's recommendations we followed has left the firm.
The proposal, which the board approved, reshapes next year's budget.
The clients that complained about delays were offered compensation.
The warehouse, who stores seasonal stock, needs new shelving.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Whose" correctly shows possession: the team belongs to the manager.

Tip: If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose."

FALSE — You need possession, not "who is": write "whose recommendations."

Tip: "Who's" = who is / who has; "whose" = of whom / of which.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" with commas correctly adds non-essential detail about the proposal.

Tip: Extra information between commas takes "which" for things, never "that."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for people is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: In defining clauses about people, "who" sounds slightly more formal than "that."

FALSE — A warehouse is not a person; use "which": "The warehouse, which stores…"

Tip: Animate-looking nouns that are still things take "which," not "who."
tasks.solution_overview: Possession and person/thing choice dominate this set. Separate "who's" (contraction) from "whose" (belonging), and keep "who" for people while "which" covers places, buildings, and documents.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The merger, that investors feared, went through quietly.
The consultant whom we hired last spring redesigned the workflow.
The software which crashes during peak hours needs a patch.
The director who we briefed yesterday asked for more data.
The figures that the CFO presented them surprised the panel.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A comma-bound clause must use "which," not "that": "The merger, which investors feared…"

Tip: Spot the commas first; they ban "that" in careful British exam English.

TRUE — Formal "whom" correctly marks the object of "hired."

Tip: If the relative would be "him/her/them," "whom" is the careful choice.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines which software; no commas required.

Tip: British formal writing often prefers "which" even in defining clauses about things.

TRUE — Informal/object "who" is widely accepted here; the sentence is grammatical as written.

Tip: Exams may still prefer "whom" after a preposition, but bare object "who" is usually fine.

FALSE — Remove the residual "them": "The figures that the CFO presented surprised…"

Tip: The relative already equals the object; a second object pronoun is always wrong.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch non-restrictive "that," object relatives (who/whom), and pronoun leftovers. If the clause already does the object’s job, nothing else should sit in that slot.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The trainee who joined in March already leads client calls.
The guidelines that HR published apply to remote staff.
The factory whose output doubled last quarter needs overtime cover.
The speaker who's opening the conference arrives at nine.
The forecast which the economists released looks optimistic.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "who" correctly identifies the trainee.

Tip: No commas when the clause is needed to pick out which person.

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which guidelines.

Tip: "That" is a safe default in restrictive clauses about things.

TRUE — "Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people.

Tip: "The factory whose output…" = "the factory’s output."

TRUE — "Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before "opening."

Tip: Try expanding the contraction; if "who is" fits, "who's" is right.

TRUE — Restrictive "which" correctly defines the forecast.

Tip: Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound models: people with "who," things with "that/which," possession with "whose," and a genuine "who's" = who is. Use them as clean reference patterns before the traps get harder.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The partner with whom we negotiate prefers evening calls.
The dataset, that includes last year's returns, is incomplete.
Anyone who's password expires must reset it today.
The branch which we visited last week is closing for renovations.
The engineer that designed the prototype will present at noon.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Preposition + "whom" is the formal, correct pattern for a person as object.

Tip: After a preposition, prefer "whom" (people) or "which" (things), not "who" or "that."

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "The dataset, which includes…"

Tip: Commas + "that" is a classic exam fail.

FALSE — Possession requires "whose": "Anyone whose password expires…"

Tip: If "who is password" sounds nonsense, you wanted "whose."

TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the branch.

Tip: Object relatives can keep "which/that" or drop the pronoun entirely in informal style.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in defining clauses.

Tip: "Who" is often preferred for people, but "that" is not an error here.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + whom is the polished form; commas still forbid "that"; and "who's" vs "whose" remains a high-frequency trap. Read each clause aloud with the contraction expanded.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The supplier from which we source packaging raised its prices.
The intern whom mentors praised completed the rotation early.
The policy that HR revised last month it now covers freelancers.
Vienna, which hosts the summit, has limited hotel capacity.
The investors who capital the startup provided later withdrew.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition.

Tip: Keep the preposition with "which/whom"; avoid ending with a stranded wrong relative.

TRUE — "Whom" correctly marks the intern as the object of "praised" (mentors praised the intern).

Tip: If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified.

FALSE — Delete residual "it": "The policy that HR revised last month now covers…"

Tip: One clause, one object slot — never both relative and "it."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Vienna.

Tip: Place names with commas almost always take "which," not "that."

FALSE — Word order collapses; write "The investors who provided the startup’s capital later withdrew."

Tip: Keep the relative clause’s internal word order like a normal statement after the relative.
tasks.solution_overview: Preposition + which, object whom, and residual pronouns dominate here. If a leftover "it" remains after the relative, cut it; if word order inside the clause collapses, rebuild the clause as a normal statement.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lawyer to whom the letter was addressed replied within a day.
The spreadsheet who's columns are locked cannot be edited.
Staff whose badges have expired must visit reception.
The museum that we toured on Friday displays modern design.
The CEO, that announced the restructure, takes questions at four.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition.

Tip: Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people in exam English.

FALSE — A spreadsheet’s columns need "whose," not "who's."

Tip: "Who's" never marks possession — expand it and the error is obvious.

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause.

Tip: "Whose" works with plural noun heads just as with singular.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which museum.

Tip: Object "that/which" can often be omitted: "The museum we toured…"

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The CEO, who announced…"

Tip: Commas + person → "who"; commas + thing → "which"; never "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whom," possession with "whose," and the ban on "that" after commas are the three checks here. Expand every "who's" before you mark the sentence true.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The invoice which accounts paid yesterday still shows the old rate.
The researcher of who the paper was co-authored declined comment.
The building that overlooks the river is under offer.
Customers which request refunds must keep their receipts.
The mentor whose advice shaped the pitch will join the rehearsal.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Defining "which" correctly identifies the invoice.

Tip: Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things.

FALSE — After a preposition referring to a person, use "whom": "of whom the paper was co-authored" (or better, rephrase).

Tip: "Of who" is almost never correct; "of whom" is the formal fix.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the building.

Tip: No commas when the clause picks out which building.

FALSE — Customers are people; use "who" or "that," not "which."

Tip: "Which" for people is a strong red flag in exam marking.

TRUE — "Whose advice" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: People vs things and preposition + whom are the focus. Never use "which" for customers or staff, and never leave "of who" after a preposition.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The minutes, which the secretary circulated, confirm the vote.
The candidate whom the panel shortlisted withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still waiting should check the board outside.
The algorithm that ranks applications was updated overnight.
The office in which the interview takes place is on the third floor.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known minutes.

Tip: If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right.

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly follows the panel as subject of "shortlisted."

Tip: Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified.

TRUE — "Who's" = "who is" before "still waiting."

Tip: Expand the contraction; if the sentence still works, keep "who's."

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the algorithm.

Tip: Technical nouns take the same who/which/that rules as everyday ones.

TRUE — "In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place.

Tip: Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical.
tasks.solution_overview: These are clean mid-level models: non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which." Compare them with nearby traps before you lock your answers.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bond, that matures next June, was issued at a discount.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk 12.
Products whose labels lack allergen warnings must be recalled.
The witness who the prosecutor called seemed unsure.
The framework on which the appraisal rests needs revision.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "which" after commas: "The bond, which matures next June…"

Tip: Financial nouns follow the same comma rule as any other thing.

FALSE — After "to," use "whom": "to whom complaints should be sent."

Tip: Preposition + who is almost always wrong; make it "whom."

TRUE — "Whose" correctly marks possession for products/labels.

Tip: "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English.

TRUE — Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person called.

Tip: Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object is not marked wrong in most exams.

TRUE — "On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Keep preposition + which together in formal answers.
tasks.solution_overview: Comma + "that," "to who," and possession for things are the main traps. Formal preposition + which/whom patterns earn easy true marks when you spot them.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The auditors with who we share draft findings signed an NDA.
London, which remains our European hub, will host the kick-off.
The dossier that compliance flagged contains personal data.
A colleague who's been seconded to Berlin still joins our stand-ups.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the stress check.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whom" after "with": "with whom we share draft findings."

Tip: Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about London.

Tip: City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who."

TRUE — Defining "that" correctly restricts which dossier.

Tip: Compliance and legal nouns follow ordinary relative rules.

TRUE — "Who's been" = "who has been," a correct present-perfect relative.

Tip: "Who's" covers both "who is" and "who has."

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail about the prototype.

Tip: If the noun is already identified, commas + "which" are the pair.
tasks.solution_overview: One clear "with who" error sits among solid non-restrictive and defining models. Confirm each true sentence’s person/thing choice and comma pattern before moving on.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The broker through whom we placed the order confirmed the fill.
Equipment that arrives damaged must be photographed immediately.
The founder whose startup we acquired stays on as an adviser.
Anyone who's unsure about the dress code should ask HR.
The clause under which penalties apply is highlighted in bold.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Through whom" correctly marks a person after a preposition.

Tip: Formal business English loves preposition + whom for intermediaries.

TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines which equipment.

Tip: Uncountable heads still take normal relative pronouns.

TRUE — "Whose startup" correctly shows possession.

Tip: "Whose" + noun phrase is the standard possessive relative.

TRUE — "Who's unsure" = "who is unsure."

Tip: If "who is" fits cleanly, "who's" is not a possession error.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Legal "under which" / "pursuant to which" patterns are exam favourites.
tasks.solution_overview: All five showcase reliable formal relatives: preposition + whom/which, defining "that," possessive "whose," and a legitimate "who's." Treat them as templates for harder items.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The committee appointed a chairperson that her experience was unmatched.
Negotiators on whom the deadline weighed most heavily requested an extension.
The portal which applicants use it times out after ten minutes.
Berlin, that we visited for the trade fair, has excellent rail links.
Shareholders whom voted against the motion still attended the lunch.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Use "whose": "a chairperson whose experience was unmatched," not "that her."

Tip: "That + possessive determiner" is a broken relative; switch to "whose."

TRUE — "On whom" correctly places a person after a preposition.

Tip: If stress falls on people as the object of a preposition, "whom" is the formal form.

FALSE — Remove "it": "The portal which applicants use times out…"

Tip: Residual object pronouns after relatives are always wrong.

FALSE — Non-restrictive place names need "which": "Berlin, which we visited…"

Tip: Commas + "that" fail for cities just as for documents.

FALSE — Subject relative needs "who": "Shareholders who voted…"

Tip: "Whom" is never the subject of the relative clause’s verb.
tasks.solution_overview: Harder traps mix broken possession ("that her"), leftover pronouns, non-restrictive "that," and subject "whom." Only the preposition + whom sentence is clean here.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The vendor with whose terms we disagreed still won the tender.
Delegates for who travel was arranged must collect vouchers by noon.
The archive in which older contracts are stored is being digitised.
A process that we streamlined last year now saves two hours a week.
The economist who's forecast we cited later revised her numbers.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whose terms" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "Preposition + whose + noun" is formal but fully grammatical.

FALSE — Use "whom": "Delegates for whom travel was arranged…"

Tip: After "for/to/with/from," person-relatives need "whom."

TRUE — "In which" correctly marks a place after a preposition.

Tip: Formal answers prefer "in which" over "where" in some exam styles.

TRUE — Defining "that" (object) correctly identifies the process.

Tip: Object "that/which" can be omitted: "A process we streamlined…"

FALSE — Possession needs "whose": "The economist whose forecast we cited…"

Tip: "Who's forecast" expands to nonsense; that signals "whose."
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced patterns include "with whose" and "in which," while "for who" and "who's + noun" remain frequent fails. Expand every contraction before you judge possession.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The only applicant that the firm shortlisted declined the offer.
Our Helsinki office, that opened in 2018, now employs forty people.
Investors to whom the prospectus was mailed raised further questions.
The dashboard which tracks liquidity it refreshes every minute.
Teams whose KPIs slipped this quarter must submit a recovery plan.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Restrictive "that" correctly defines the only shortlisted applicant.

Tip: "The only / the first / the last + that" is a natural defining pattern.

FALSE — Non-restrictive needs "which": "Our Helsinki office, which opened…"

Tip: Named, unique offices take commas + "which," not "that."

TRUE — "To whom" correctly marks recipients after a preposition.

Tip: Mail/send/address + to whom is a standard formal relative.

FALSE — Drop "it": "The dashboard which tracks liquidity refreshes…"

Tip: The relative clause already contains its object/subject logic; no second pronoun.

TRUE — "Whose KPIs" correctly shows possession for teams.

Tip: Collective nouns still take "whose" for belonging.
tasks.solution_overview: Defining "the only… that," formal "to whom," and "whose" for teams are solid; commas + "that" and residual "it" are the fails. Prioritise comma diagnosis first.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The regulator by whom the fine was imposed published guidance today.
Candidates which fail the compliance quiz cannot access the portal.
A policy whose wording is ambiguous invites disputes.
The seminar at which we presented drew a large audience.
Someone who's ID badge is missing should report to security.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "By whom" correctly marks the agent in a formal relative.

Tip: Passive-related "by whom" is formal but grammatical.

FALSE — People need "who/that": "Candidates who fail…"

Tip: Never use "which" for candidates, clients, or staff.

TRUE — "Whose wording" correctly marks possession for a policy.

Tip: Documents and policies commonly take "whose" in exam English.

TRUE — "At which" correctly attaches the preposition to an event.

Tip: Prefer "at which / in which" over informal "where" in formal answers when asked.

FALSE — Use "whose": "Someone whose ID badge is missing…"

Tip: "Who's ID" = "who is ID," which never works.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "by whom" / "at which" sit beside people-"which" and "who's + noun" errors. Keep person/thing and contraction checks automatic at this level.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The partner in whom's firm we invested later exited the market.
Few of the metrics on which the bonus depends are under our control.
The analyst that her model underestimated demand has revised it.
Board members whom the chair thanked stayed for photographs.
The warehouse where stock is held, that flooded last spring, is closed.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Malformed possession; write "The partner in whose firm we invested…"

Tip: Never stack "whom's"; use "whose" after the preposition.

TRUE — "On which" correctly links metrics after a preposition.

Tip: "The X on which Y depends" is a high-value formal pattern.

FALSE — Replace "that her" with "whose": "The analyst whose model underestimated…"

Tip: "That + possessive" always signals a missing "whose."

TRUE — Object "whom" correctly refers to the members thanked.

Tip: Subject of main clause + object relative "whom" is a clean formal structure.

FALSE — Mixing "where" with a second non-restrictive "that" is wrong; prefer "The warehouse where stock is held, which flooded last spring, is closed."

Tip: A second relative after commas still cannot be "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Top-band items twist possession after prepositions and stack relatives. Reject "whom's" and "that her," keep "on which," and remember a second comma-bound clause still wants "which."

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lender to whose conditions we agreed released the funds.
Staff for whom remote work was approved must log hours weekly.
The prototype that the engineers dismantled it cannot be reassembled.
Singapore, which we use as our APAC base, hosts the regional board.
Anyone who's completed module three may sit the assessment.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "To whose conditions" correctly combines preposition and possession.

Tip: "To/with/under whose + noun" is advanced but correct.

TRUE — "For whom" correctly marks people after a preposition.

Tip: Approval/arrangement phrases often need "for whom."

FALSE — Remove "it": "The prototype that the engineers dismantled cannot be reassembled."

Tip: Even in long sentences, residual objects are still errors.

TRUE — Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about Singapore.

Tip: Country/city names with commas take "which."

TRUE — "Who's completed" = "who has completed."

Tip: Present-perfect "who's" is possession’s innocent twin — expand to check.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "to whose" / "for whom" are trustworthy when the grammar fits; the leftover "it" is the only clear fail. Expand "who's" once more to confirm "who has."

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The counsel of whom we sought advice later joined the opposing side.
A clause that its purpose is unclear should be redrafted.
Partners who the firm promoted last year now lead regional desks.
The platform via which clients upload documents went offline at noon.
The interim CFO, that arrived in May, reorganised the treasury team.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Of whom" correctly marks the person after the preposition in a formal relative.

Tip: "Of whom we sought advice" is stiff but exam-correct.

FALSE — Use "whose": "A clause whose purpose is unclear…"

Tip: "That its" is the same broken pattern as "that her."

TRUE — Object "who" for people promoted is acceptable modern usage.

Tip: Formal alternatives use "whom"; both are usually accepted without a preceding preposition.

TRUE — "Via which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing.

Tip: Tech/process nouns take "which" after prepositions, not "who."

FALSE — Non-restrictive about a person needs "who": "The interim CFO, who arrived…"

Tip: Title + commas still bans "that."
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "of whom" / "via which" contrast with "that its" and comma + "that" about a person. Diagnose possession failures and non-restrictive person clauses first.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The underwriters with whom we placed the issue required further disclosure.
Anyone whose laptop holds client files must enable full-disk encryption.
The jurisdiction under which the dispute will be heard is specified in clause 19.
A consultant who's already briefed the board need not attend the dry run.
The metrics against which performance is judged were agreed last autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "With whom" correctly marks people after a preposition in a defining clause.

Tip: Placement/issuance language often uses "with whom we placed…"

TRUE — "Whose laptop" correctly shows possession.

Tip: Security policies love "anyone whose + noun" constructions.

TRUE — "Under which" correctly links the legal framework.

Tip: Contract English frequently uses "under which / pursuant to which."

TRUE — "Who's already briefed" = "who has already briefed."

Tip: Final check: expand "who's"; if "who has" fits, the sentence can stand.

TRUE — "Against which" correctly marks the standard of comparison.

Tip: "The X against which Y is judged" is a polished relative pattern.
tasks.solution_overview: A clean capstone of advanced but correct relatives: preposition + whom/which, possessive "whose," and "who's" = who has. Use these as your final checklist for person, thing, possession, and contraction.
